newsitem.title: USA: Dollar begins firm in US, sustains mild PPI damage.
newsitem.headline: Dollar begins firm in US, sustains mild PPI damage.

text.p: The dollar began U.S. trade substantially stronger against the mark and slightly firmer versus the yen on Wednesday, buoyed by lingering hopes for a hike in U.S. interest rates and broad mark weakness on the crosses.

A report from the Labor Department showing that producer prices fell by a larger than expected 0.6 percent in April led to modest weakness in the greenback, but analysts expected the damage to be short-lived.
"It doesn't help the dollar go up," said David Ethridge, director of currency analysis at MMS International.
"The pipeline is showing virtually no upside pressures but the Fed does not base its decision on the wholesale prices," he added.
The dollar opened at 1.7055/65 marks, up from Tuesday's closing rate of 1.6930/40. Dollar/yen was changing hands at 118.65/70, up modestly from 118.55/65.

Dealers said that hopes for an interest rate hike at next week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting continued to support the dollar, in spite of the producer price plunge -- the largest since August of 1993.
In overseas trade, the dollar was propped up from its lows on a combination of supportive Japanese data and remarks from key Bundesbank officials.
Japan's current account surplus dropped 17 percent in March from a year earlier to 1.03 trillion yen, the Finance Ministry said on Wednesday.

"I think that definitely had a positive impact on dollar/yen," said Ben Strauss, assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer. "It came out when we were near the lows and lent some comfort to the market."
Nevertheless, economists said the drop in the surplus could be the last for quite some time and dollar/yen was greeted with solid offers above the 119 level.

"The impression the market's been left with is that U.S. and Japanese officials are content with a 110 to 120 range so even after this large move we're at the top of the acceptable range," said Rick Gomes, foreign exchange manager at Republic National Bank of New York.
Dollar prospects against the mark, however, appeared brighter, according to dealers.
Bundesbank council members Ernst Welteke and Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher both expressed satisfaction with dollar/mark near its current level on Wednesday.
And dealers said Conference Board forecasts, released late Tuesday, which called for a rise in the dollar to 1.85 marks by early 1998 were also supportive.
Selling marks for yen continued to be a favored trade on Wednesday, with the cross touching a one-year low of 69.45.
"Europe has slammed mark/yen again here and that's why dollar/Europe is near its overnight highs whereas dollar/yen has not made much headway," said Strauss.

Dealers predicted more range consolidation between 1.69 and 1.71 marks in the near-term, with the potential for a move as high as 1.72 later in the week. They were skeptical of whether dollar/mark could get back to its cycle highs, however, for quite some time.
In other trade on Wednesday, sterling remained well-bid against the mark, holding above the 2.79 level after touching a high of 2.7975 earlier in the session.
A larger than expected fall in UK jobless figures for April and prospects for higher rates were supportive of the pound, traders said.
Sterling advanced to $1.6370/75 at the open from $1.6317/27 on Tuesday. Elsewhere, the dollar firmed to 1.4461/68 Swiss francs from 1.4355/65 and rose to Canadian $1.3876/81 from C$1.3858/63.
The Australian dollar opened at $0.7790/00, up from $0.7760/65.
((-- Noah Barkin, N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1673))
